posts.body_html: Good lord Mike, that is obscene. I thought I had a lot of flytraps. Those mass plantings look fantastic! Funny to see all those open empty traps, haha. Like Calen said, here more often than not most traps are closed around prey and sport carcasses when open. I don't know how "natural" that look is though because when I visited a flytrap site in Florida I saw very few traps with prey in them. I wonder if the same is true in their native habitat?

Let's see pics of that bowl Calen! "I showed you mine, let's see yours"...LOL! Ahem, Gotta show Damon of California Carnivores how Venus fly traps are really grown, his bowls of B-52 and Ginormous...those are for amateurs, hehe
(opens trenchcoat) Here are a couple shots of my humble B-52 bowl (nothing compared to Mike's VFT lawn lol!). These shots are from May when the overcast conditions acted like polycarb to bring out insane solid dark reds in the trap interiors (photos not quite capturing the full saturation of course...). As soon as the direct sun came out, the pigments faded! The bowl is doing well but is due for repotting this winter - seems like VFT appreciate new soil more frequently than Sarrs. Lately the raccoons have been walking on the bowl and setting off all the traps at night (shakes raised fist!) but there's no question in my mind that en-masse is the way to grow these puppies.

been a while since this thread has been updated, so here's some new pics, taken 8/18/19:

D. muscipula Onslow Co, NC. I think this is the only group of plants that I have location data to. these are the mother plants, I have divided them all and the divisons are as big as these are! Every single plant in the community pot is a different clone, and it appears there might be a giant one in the mix:


close up of the big clone:



One last shot of the Onslow Co population:



Now here's a group of unique, genetically diverse genotypes. this population is called D. muscipula 'Croatia'-these are the mother plants, and I think most of the plants in here are different clones. Pretty sure I made divisions of these as well:






D. muscipula 'Hosford.' These were introduced into Florida by Old Man Northrop in the early 1900's, so they aren't native to FL, but they are a genteic goldmine! Technically speaking, they're a non-native, invasive species, but from a different perspective, these plants contain genetics that are likely extinct in their native range. Are these destroying a natural habitat, preserving genetics that would have otherwise gone extinct, or both? You could also consider these a landrace variety, meaning these genetics have adapted to a particular new environment in Florida.

I've taken it one step further: these have been grown from seeds, and only the colorful, vigorous, and big plants were artififically selected for propagation. These genotypes can produce pretty big and colorful traps under optimal conditions that are on par with B-52! These are pictures from a while ago:


I think the red interior and green exterior of the trap is a genetic thing that is highly environmentally induced:


DANG BABY!


Some blurry pics of Royal Red starting to look nice:

posts.body_html:
Dionaea 'Ginormous.' I started off with a very, very small division of this plant, but now that it's growing pretty strong, it's producing some nice looking traps! Normally, venus fly traps don't look that great outdoors in Northern California this early in the spring, but for whatever reason, they're producing some decent looking traps. Will keep you posted on how these do, but so far, they're pretty easy to grow. I heard other reports of growers having a hard time with these, but that's probably because they were starting off with greenhouse grown plants acclimating to outdoor conditions, or maybe their starting material just didn't have good growth momentum to start. After growing dozens of venus fly trap clones, only a few have been truly difficult to grow to their fullest potential around here.

Pics taken 4/11/20:

posts.body_html:
Dionaea 'GINORMOUS.' Over the years, I've heard reports that this clone is difficult to grow and that it was 'Over-hyped' as being the next best giant venus fly trap. In my experience, this clone was difficult to get some good growth momentum started (I acquired a very tiny division years ago), but once you get it growing well, it takes off! No need for greenhouse conditions to get this clone to do well, it performs very well outdoors here in Northern California! My plants aren't yet producing giant traps, but that's because the "bulbs" haven't had a chance to size up yet....they'll probably get really big next year if they continue growing well.

Consistently deep red traps is an added plus! Pics taken 7/30/20:
